Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: This item is the only maladaptive strategy that is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile. The threat items describe classic hypervigilant danger-monitoring (false alarms, waking to check safety, inability to relax), and the other strategy items reflect avoidance/concealment consistent with feeling unsafe. In contrast, deliberately seeking conflict or creating drama as a distraction points toward an externalizing/interpersonal regulation pattern that is not supported anywhere else in the selected triggers, memory, appraisal, or threat content. Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies should be tightly linked; this strategy does not plausibly arise from the specific threat pattern provided and makes the profile internally less coherent.

vignette:
Mariam was 50, a divorced Middle Eastern woman who had built a life in the United States around helping other displaced families, yet the knowledge that shaped her work also carried the weight of what had happened to her. Years earlier, when she was fleeing as a refugee, there had been a night at a border crossing when armed men shouted at the group she was with, ordered everyone to stand still, and searched bags under harsh lights while children cried and people were pushed and separated. Mariam had been forced to keep her head down and wait, listening for her own name to be called, certain that a wrong movement could mean detention or worse. The memory that stayed with her was not only the violence itself but the helpless watchfulness of it: the bright beam on the road, the sudden voices, the sense that danger could appear from anywhere and that she had to notice it first.

In the years that followed, Mariam found that her body kept behaving as if that border were still near. She often reacted as though something terrible was happening even in ordinary situations, jumping at a dropped tray in a clinic waiting room or feeling a rush of fear when someone approached her too quickly from behind. At night she would wake fully alert, checking the locks and listening for sounds in the hallway, and even in her own apartment she could not settle into sleep with any ease. She described being unable to relax even when she knew she was safe, as though safety were only temporary and might be revoked at any moment. Those moments of false alarm left her ashamed, but they also convinced her that she was still vulnerable and needed to stay ready.

That constant sense of danger gradually shaped the way Mariam moved through daily life. She had come to believe that if she let herself feel too much, her fear would become overwhelming and impossible to manage, so she worked hard to avoid strong emotional situations whenever she could. At work as a social worker, she began stepping back from the most distressing refugee intakes and keeping conversations practical, because stories that resembled her own could leave her shaken for hours. She also started wearing concealing clothing, choosing looser layers and longer sleeves so she would not stand out in public or draw attention in crowded places. More than once she noticed herself scanning the environment as she entered a grocery store, a mosque event, or the waiting room at her office, looking for exits, watching hands, and mentally mapping who might pose a risk. In her mind, these habits were not overreactions but precautions; if she stayed unnoticed and stayed alert, she might avoid being caught off guard again.

Yet the effort to stay protected also kept her alarm system on constant watch. Because she was scanning every room and bracing against anything that might stir strong feeling, nearly any unfamiliar glance, raised voice, or sudden movement could register as a possible threat, and the body-wide tension that followed made her even more certain danger was near. Mariam noticed that the more she tried to avoid emotional stress and the more she monitored people and places for signs of danger, the more often she found herself reacting as if something was wrong when nothing actually was. A colleague turning too quickly in the office, a child yelling in the lobby, or a man standing near the door after dark could send her heart racing and pull her back into the same fixed vigilance she had felt years before. She was careful not to tell many people how much energy it took to get through a day, but the strain was visible in how guarded she had become, how little she socialized, and how often she left work feeling exhausted by the effort of staying composed.

By the time she came for help, Mariam was worried not only about the memories of the border crossing but about how narrow her life had become around them. She wanted to keep doing her work without feeling as though every hallway, street, and room might turn dangerous, and she was most afraid that the constant checking and retreat would keep tightening until she no longer trusted her own sense of safety at all.
